unit-alg-t4-01.title: Topic 4 · 4-1 Inverse Variation and the Reciprocal Function
unit-alg-t4-01.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 4-1: Inverse Variation and the Reciprocal Function

summary.text: Lesson 4-1 introduces inverse variation, y = k/x, and its graph: how to recognise an inverse variation from a table, find and use the constant of variation, and graph the reciprocal function f(x) = 1/x and its translations, with their asymptotes, domain and range.

why.text: Inverse variation describes every trade-off where one thing goes up exactly as another comes down — speed and travel time, workers and hours, pressure and volume. And the graph of 1/x is the parent of every rational function in this topic.

objectives.text: Decide whether a table or a situation is an inverse variation by checking that xy is constant
Write an inverse variation equation from one pair of values and use it to find another
Graph y = 1/x and its translations, and state their asymptotes, domain and range
Tell inverse variation apart from direct variation and from a line that simply decreases

parentNote.text: Two things trip students up here. First, treating any decreasing pattern as inverse variation — the test is that the PRODUCT xy stays constant, and one question deliberately offers a table where three of four products agree. Second, the sign inside the denominator: 1/(x + 3) moves the graph LEFT. One thing worth knowing: the textbook's own practice includes "gas left in a tank varies inversely with miles driven", which is not actually an inverse variation (the tank empties at a steady rate, a falling line). This unit teaches it as the counter-example; if her class marks it the book's way, that is worth a word with her teacher.

nextUp.text: Start with the table test — multiply every column — then the translated graphs.

cards.def:
**A relationship of the form y = k/x, with k ≠ 0: multiply one variable by a number and the other is divided by that same number.**
• Double x and y halves; triple x and y drops to a third.
• Said aloud: "y varies inversely as x".
cards.hint: One goes up by a FACTOR, the other comes down by the same factor.

cards.def:
**The number k = xy that every pair in an inverse variation shares.**
• One known pair is enough to find it: multiply the two values.
• Once you have k, any other value is k divided by the one you know.
cards.hint: Find k first, every time — it is the whole relationship in one number.

cards.def:
**Multiply x by y in EVERY column; it is an inverse variation only if every product is the same.**
• One column that breaks the pattern is enough to rule it out.
• Checking two or three columns and stopping is how a near-miss table slips through.
cards.hint: Every column, not just the first few.

cards.def:
**Direct variation keeps the RATIO y/x constant; inverse variation keeps the PRODUCT xy constant.**
• Direct: y = kx, and the two variables rise and fall together.
• Inverse: y = k/x, and as one rises the other falls.
cards.hint: Ratio for direct, product for inverse.

cards.def:
**A table where y goes down as x goes up is not automatically an inverse variation — the product xy still has to stay constant.**
• x: 1, 2, 3, 4 with y: 20, 16, 12, 8 falls steadily, but its products are 20, 32, 36, 32. That is a straight line going down, not an inverse variation.
• Inverse variation falls fast at first and then ever more slowly; it never reaches zero.
cards.hint: Steady drops by the same AMOUNT are linear, not inverse.

cards.def:
**f(x) = 1/x sends every nonzero number to its reciprocal; its graph is two separate branches, in quadrants I and III.**
• It is the simplest inverse variation, with k = 1.
• Near 0 the values blow up; far from 0 they shrink toward 0.
cards.hint: Two branches, because x = 0 splits the graph in half.

cards.def:
**A line that a graph gets closer and closer to as it runs off along it.**
• A vertical asymptote marks an x-value the function can never use.
• A horizontal asymptote describes where the values settle as x runs far left and far right.
cards.hint: The graph hugs it more and more tightly.

cards.def:
**Vertical asymptote x = 0, horizontal asymptote y = 0; domain all x ≠ 0, range all y ≠ 0.**
• As x → ±∞, f(x) → 0. As x → 0 from the right, f(x) → +∞; from the left, f(x) → −∞.
• It never touches y = 0, because 1/x = 0 would need 1 = 0.
cards.hint: The two axes are the two asymptotes.

cards.def:
**y = k/x with k < 0 puts the two branches in quadrants II and IV instead of I and III.**
• It is the k > 0 graph flipped over the x-axis.
• The asymptotes do not move: still x = 0 and y = 0.
cards.hint: A negative k flips the picture; it never moves the asymptotes.

cards.def:
**y = a/(x − h) + k is 1/x moved h units horizontally and k units vertically, so its asymptotes are x = h and y = k.**
• Domain: every x except h. Range: every y except k.
• The point (h, k), where the two asymptotes cross, is the centre the two branches curl around.
cards.hint: The asymptotes move with the graph — read them straight off h and k.

cards.term: The sign trap in x − h
cards.def:
**In 1/(x + 3), h is −3: the vertical asymptote is x = −3, to the LEFT.**
• x + 3 = x − (−3). The number inside moves the graph the opposite way to its sign.
• The k outside does what it says: + 4 is up 4, − 4 is down 4.
cards.hint: Inside the denominator, the sign lies; outside, it tells the truth.

cards.def:
**Find k from the pair you are given, then divide k by the new value.**
• Check it makes sense: if one quantity got bigger, the other must have got smaller.
• If your answer moved in the same direction, you treated it as direct variation by mistake.

**y = k/x² means y is divided by the SQUARE of whatever x is multiplied by.**
• Multiply x by 2 and y is divided by 4; multiply x by 5 and y is divided by 25.
• Light and sound fade with distance this way.
cards.hint: Square the scale factor before you divide.

questions.q: Which equation models an inverse variation?
questions.hint: Look for the variable in the denominator with a constant on top.
steps: An inverse variation has the form y = k/x with k ≠ 0.
y = 9x and y = x/9 are both direct variations: y is a constant times x.
y = 9 − x falls as x rises, but it is linear, not inverse.
Only y = 9/x has the form k/x.

ex.main: **y = 9/x.** Here k = 9, so every pair multiplies to 9. y = 9x and y = x/9 are direct variations, where the ratio stays fixed, and y = 9 − x is a falling line: it decreases, but its products do not stay constant.
ex.tip: Decreasing is not the test. The product is.

questions.q: In an inverse variation y = k/x, what stays the same for every pair of values?
questions.hint: Rearrange y = k/x so k stands alone.
steps: Start from y = k/x.
Multiply both sides by x: xy = k.
k is a constant, so xy is the same for every pair.
The product xy stays the same.

ex.main: **The product xy.** Multiplying y = k/x through by x gives xy = k. A constant RATIO is the mark of direct variation, which is the commonest mix-up here.
ex.tip: Ratio for direct, product for inverse.

questions.q: What are the asymptotes of f(x) = 1/x?
questions.hint: Which x can you never use, and where do the values settle far out?
steps: 1/x is undefined at x = 0, so x = 0 is a vertical asymptote.
As x runs far left or right, 1/x shrinks toward 0.
So y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote.
The asymptotes are x = 0 and y = 0.

ex.main: **x = 0 and y = 0.** The function cannot use x = 0, and far out its values close in on 0 without reaching it, so both axes are asymptotes. y = x and y = −x are the graph's lines of symmetry, not lines it approaches.
ex.tip: For 1/x the two axes ARE the two asymptotes.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/x?
questions.hint: Which input makes the denominator zero?
steps: The domain is every x the function can accept.
Division by zero is undefined.
x = 0 is the only input that puts 0 in the denominator.
The domain is all real numbers except 0.

ex.main: **All real numbers except 0.** Negative inputs are fine — 1/(−4) = −0.25 — which is exactly why the graph has a branch on the left. Only 0 is excluded.
ex.tip: Excluded x-values come from the denominator and nowhere else.

questions.q: Which set of pairs is an inverse variation?
questions.hint: Multiply each x by its own y, all the way along.
steps: Products for 3, 4, 6, 8 with 16, 12, 8, 6: 48, 48, 48, 48 — constant.
Products for 1, 2, 4, 8 with 24, 12, 8, 3: 24, 24, 32, 24 — one column breaks it.
1, 2, 3, 4 with 20, 16, 12, 8 falls by a steady 4, which is linear: products 20, 32, 36, 32.
2, 4, 6, 8 with 5, 10, 15, 20 rises together with x — direct variation.
Only x: 3, 4, 6, 8 with y: 16, 12, 8, 6 keeps xy = 48.

ex.main: **x: 3, 4, 6, 8 with y: 16, 12, 8, 6.** Every product is 48. The 24, 12, 8, 3 set is the trap: three of its four products are 24, and the column 4 × 8 = 32 rules it out. The steadily falling set is a line, and the rising set is direct variation.
ex.tip: Check every column. Three out of four is still a no.

questions.q: What is the vertical asymptote of g(x) = 1/(x − 6) + 2?
questions.hint: Which x-value makes the denominator zero?
steps: The vertical asymptote sits where x − 6 = 0.
Solve: x = 6.
The + 2 outside the fraction moves the graph up; it does not touch the vertical asymptote.
The vertical asymptote is x = 6.

ex.main: **x = 6.** It is the one input that makes the denominator 0. Answering x = −6 flips the sign inside the denominator, and x = 2 reads the vertical shift as if it were the horizontal one.
ex.tip: Set the denominator equal to zero — it beats remembering a sign rule.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of h(x) = 5/(x + 4) − 7?
questions.hint: Where do the values settle as x runs far out?
steps: As x runs far left or right, 5/(x + 4) shrinks toward 0.
So h(x) settles toward 0 − 7.
That level is the horizontal asymptote.
The horizontal asymptote is y = −7.

ex.main: **y = −7.** The fraction fades to 0 far out, leaving only the − 7. The 5 stretches the branches but moves no asymptote, and the + 4 inside sets the VERTICAL asymptote, x = −4.
ex.tip: The number added outside the fraction is the horizontal asymptote, sign and all.

questions.q: x and y vary inversely, and y = 6 when x = 8. What is y when x = 12?
questions.hint: Find k first.
steps: So y = 48/x.

ex.main: **4.** k = 48, and 48 ÷ 12 = 4. Check the direction: x went up, so y had to come down. 9 is what direct variation would give (y rising with x), and 10 adds the change in x onto y as if the relationship were a line.
ex.tip: If your answer moved the same way as x, it was not inverse variation.

questions.q: x and y vary inversely, and y = 4 when x = −5. Which equation models the relationship?
questions.hint: k is the product of the pair, and signs come along.
steps: Substitute into y = k/x.

ex.main: **y = −20/x.** The product is negative, so k is negative. −0.8 is y ÷ x — the ratio, which belongs to direct variation, whether you then put it in the denominator or not.
ex.tip: Keep the sign: a negative k puts the branches in quadrants II and IV.

questions.q: The time to fill a tank varies inversely with the flow rate. At 15 gallons per minute it takes 32 minutes. How long does it take at 24 gallons per minute?
questions.hint: Faster flow means less time — find k, then divide.
steps: k = rate × time = 15 × 32 = 480 gallons (the size of the tank).
time = 480 ÷ rate.
At 24 gallons per minute: 480 ÷ 24.
It takes 20 minutes.

ex.main: **20 minutes.** Here k is the tank's volume, 480 gallons, which is exactly why rate × time stays fixed. 51.2 minutes multiplies as if faster flow took LONGER, 23 subtracts the change in rate, and 0.05 divides the wrong way round.
ex.tip: Ask what k means in the situation — it makes the set-up obvious.

questions.q: What are the domain and range of f(x) = 3/(x − 1) + 4?
questions.hint: The domain misses the vertical asymptote; the range misses the horizontal one.
steps: The vertical asymptote is where x − 1 = 0: x = 1.
So the domain is every x except 1.
The horizontal asymptote is the + 4: y = 4, a value the graph never reaches.
Domain: x ≠ 1. Range: y ≠ 4.

ex.main: **Domain x ≠ 1, range y ≠ 4.** For a translated reciprocal function the excluded x is the vertical asymptote and the excluded y is the horizontal one. The 3 is a stretch: it changes how steep the branches are, not which values they miss.
ex.tip: Domain ↔ vertical asymptote; range ↔ horizontal asymptote.

questions.q: How does the graph of g(x) = 1/(x + 3) − 5 relate to the graph of f(x) = 1/x?
steps: So h = −3: a horizontal shift of 3 units left.
k = −5: a vertical shift of 5 units down.
g is f moved left 3 and down 5.

ex.main: **Left 3 and down 5.** The new asymptotes are x = −3 and y = −5. "Right 3" is the sign trap inside the denominator; swapping 3 and 5 mixes up which number belongs to which direction.
ex.tip: Check by finding the vertical asymptote: x + 3 = 0 at x = −3, which is to the left.

questions.q: Which function has asymptotes x = −2 and y = 6?
questions.hint: Build it from y = 1/(x − h) + k with h = −2 and k = 6.
steps: A vertical asymptote at x = −2 means h = −2.
x − (−2) is x + 2, so the denominator is x + 2.
A horizontal asymptote at y = 6 means k = 6, added outside.

ex.main: **y = 1/(x + 2) + 6.** Its denominator is zero at x = −2 and it settles toward 6. The x − 2 version puts the vertical asymptote at x = 2, the x + 6 version swaps the two numbers, and the − 6 version puts the horizontal asymptote at y = −6.
ex.tip: Test each option by setting its denominator to zero — quicker than a rule.

questions.q: The graph shown is a translation of y = 1/x, with its asymptotes drawn in. Which equation does it show?
questions.hint: Read the two asymptote lines first, then build the equation from them.
steps: The vertical asymptote is the line x = 2, so h = 2 and the denominator is x − 2.
The horizontal asymptote is the line y = −1, so k = −1.
The branches sit top-right and bottom-left of the centre, so a is positive.

ex.main: **y = 1/(x − 2) − 1.** The asymptotes cross at (2, −1), and that crossing point is (h, k). The x + 2 option would sit left of the y-axis, the + 1 option above the x-axis, and the last swaps the two numbers.
ex.tip: The crossing point of the asymptotes is (h, k) — find it and the equation writes itself.

questions.q: y varies inversely as the square of x. If x is multiplied by 3, what happens to y?
questions.hint: Write y = k/x², then put 3x in place of x.
steps: The relationship is y = k/x².
Replace x with 3x: k/(3x)² = k/(9x²).
That is the old y divided by 9.
y is divided by 9.

ex.main: **y is divided by 9.** The scale factor on x gets squared before it divides: 3² = 9. "Divided by 3" is ordinary inverse variation, which forgets the square; "multiplied by 9" forgets that it is inverse.
ex.tip: Square the factor, then divide by it.

questions.q: Why can the graph of y = 4/x never touch the line y = 0?
opts: Because y = 0 is the vertical asymptote of the graph
Because x = 0 is excluded from the domain of the function
Because the graph only appears in the first quadrant
Solving 4/x = 0 would need 4 = 0, which is impossible
questions.hint: Try to solve 4/x = 0 and see what happens.
steps: Touching y = 0 would mean 4/x = 0 for some x.
Multiply both sides by x: 4 = 0 · x = 0.
4 = 0 is false for every x, so there is no such point.
A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, and 4 never is.

ex.main: **Because 4/x = 0 would need 4 = 0.** A fraction is zero only when its numerator is. "x = 0 is excluded" is true, but it explains the VERTICAL asymptote, not this horizontal one. The graph also has a third-quadrant branch, and y = 0 is horizontal, not vertical.
ex.tip: Vertical asymptotes come from the denominator; this one comes from the numerator never being 0.

questions.q: Which pair of quantities genuinely varies inversely?
opts: The time to drive a fixed 120 miles, and your average speed
The gas left in a tank, and the miles driven since filling it
The cost of some apples, and how many pounds you buy
A child's age, and the child's height
questions.hint: For each pair ask: is the PRODUCT fixed, whatever the values?
steps: Speed × time = distance, and the distance is fixed at 120 miles, so the product never changes.
Gas left goes DOWN by about the same amount every mile — that is a falling line, and at 0 miles an inverse variation would need infinite gas.
Apples cost more the more you buy: the ratio is fixed, so that is direct variation.
Age and height both rise, but neither their ratio nor their product is fixed.
Only speed and time for a fixed trip vary inversely.

ex.main: **Driving time and speed over a fixed 120 miles.** Their product is always 120, so doubling the speed halves the time. The gas-in-the-tank pair is a trap: it decreases, but by a fixed amount per mile, which makes it linear. An inverse variation would need the tank to hold infinite gas before the trip began.
ex.tip: Something going down is not enough. Ask what stays fixed.

questions.q: A table pairs x = 2, 3, 6, 9 with y = 27, 18, 9, 5. A classmate says it is an inverse variation because y always falls as x rises. Which verdict is right?
opts: Inverse: y falls every single time that x rises in the table
Not inverse: 9 × 5 = 45 breaks the product of 54 the other columns share
Inverse: three of the four products agree, which is close enough
Not inverse: the y-values do not fall by the same amount each time
questions.hint: Multiply every column. All of them.
steps: One product disagrees, so xy is not constant.
It is not an inverse variation, and the last column is the reason.

ex.main: **Not inverse — 9 × 5 = 45 breaks the pattern.** Falling as x rises is necessary but not sufficient, and "close enough" is not a test. The "same amount each time" verdict is right for the wrong reason: a steady drop by the same amount would make it LINEAR, which is not what inverse variation needs.
ex.tip: A right verdict with a wrong reason costs marks on a written answer.

questions.q: The number of identical pumps and the time needed to drain a pond vary inversely. Six pumps drain it in 10 hours. How many pumps are needed to drain it in 4 hours?
questions.hint: Less time needs MORE pumps — find k first.
steps: k = pumps × hours = 6 × 10 = 60 pump-hours of work.
pumps = 60 ÷ hours.
For 4 hours: 60 ÷ 4.
15 pumps.

ex.main: **15 pumps.** The job is 60 pump-hours whichever way you split it. 2.4 treats it as direct variation, so cutting the time would cut the pumps — the opposite of what happens. 40 multiplies 10 by 4, and 12 just doubles the pumps.
ex.tip: Name k in words — "pump-hours" — and the set-up stops being guesswork.

questions.q: A $240 bus rental is split equally, so each share is 240/n dollars for n people. A group of 12 is joined by 4 more people. By how much does each person's share drop?
questions.hint: Work out the share before and after; do not guess from the 4.
steps: Before: 240 ÷ 12 = $20 each.
After: 240 ÷ 16 = $15 each.
The drop is $20 − $15.
Each share drops by $5.

ex.main: **$5.** The share falls from $20 to $15. $15 is the new share rather than the drop, $4 assumes each extra person knocks a dollar off, and $1.25 is 20 ÷ 16. The jump from 12 to 16 people is a third more people, but the share falls by only a quarter — inverse variation never moves in equal steps.
ex.tip: With inverse variation, compute both values; equal steps in one never mean equal steps in the other.
